benzodiazepines.summary: Benzodiazepines are depressant medicines that slow the central nervous system, and diazepam is the member covered on this site. The MHRA says dependence can occur with therapeutic doses and can become established within weeks. MedlinePlus says diazepam is used to relieve anxiety, to control agitation caused by alcohol withdrawal, to control muscle spasms and stiffness caused by certain nerve disorders and to control seizures. The NHS describes diazepam as generally for short-term use, because longer use can cause addiction and withdrawal symptoms.
benzodiazepines.mechanism: NHS Inform describes benzodiazepines as drugs that slow down the central nervous system. MedlinePlus says diazepam, as a benzodiazepine, works by calming abnormal overactivity in the brain. A review in the NIH's PubMed Central archive says benzodiazepines act mainly on the GABA-A receptor. NHS inform says tolerance can develop quickly with frequent use. The same review says regular use can cause physical and psychological dependence, with withdrawal resembling alcohol withdrawal; NHS inform adds that stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal effects that could be life-threatening.
classEffects: The NHS lists feeling drowsy, tired or less alert among the common side effects of diazepam.
Serious side effects of diazepam are rare; the NHS lists allergic reactions, slow or shallow breathing and yellowing of the skin or eyes.
cautions: The NHS advises against alcohol and grapefruit juice while taking diazepam because they can increase the risk of side effects.

The NHS says diazepam should not be taken in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it. The manufacturer's patient leaflet says that regular use during pregnancy may cause withdrawal symptoms in the baby.
NHS Inform says combining benzodiazepines with alcohol, gabapentinoids or opioids raises the risk of overdose.
NHS Inform says stopping benzodiazepines suddenly can cause withdrawal effects that could be life-threatening.
Licensed benzodiazepines such as diazepam, lorazepam and clonazepam are Class C drugs listed in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations.

NHS inform says benzodiazepines mixed with other depressants such as alcohol, gabapentin and opioids can pose serious health risks, and advises against taking other drugs or more benzodiazepines to deal with withdrawal symptoms.
NHS inform says that for people who have used benzodiazepines for a shorter period, reducing use gradually can greatly ease unpleasant withdrawal symptoms.
In an emergency, such as a suspected overdose or severe withdrawal, call 999; NHS 111 or the GP can advise urgently; Samaritans on 116 123 is free at any time.

references.title: PMC: Benzodiazepines: Uses, Dangers, and Clinical Considerations

z-drugs.summary: Z-drugs are sleeping medicines used for insomnia, and zopiclone is the member covered on this site. NICE technology appraisal TA77 covers zaleplon, zolpidem and zopiclone for short-term insomnia. The NHS describes zopiclone as a prescription-only sleeping medicine for short-term treatment of severe insomnia. MedlinePlus warns that zolpidem can cause serious, possibly life-threatening sleep behaviours, such as driving while not fully awake, without remembering it afterwards.
z-drugs.mechanism: The NHS says zopiclone boosts the effect of GABA, a calming chemical in the brain. A StatPearls review says zolpidem binds preferentially to one benzodiazepine receptor subtype, whereas benzodiazepines act on all subtypes. NICE says that, as with benzodiazepines, the sedative effects of the Z-drugs may persist into the next day.
classEffects: The NHS lists a dry mouth, a bitter or metallic taste, and feeling sleepy or tired the next day as common side effects of zopiclone.
The NHS lists sleepwalking, or doing things such as making food or phone calls while asleep, and a serious allergic reaction as possible serious side effects of zopiclone.
cautions: The NHS says alcohol with zopiclone can cause very deep sleep, so that breathing is not normal and waking is very difficult.
The NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery for 12 hours after taking zopiclone.
The NHS says the body gets used to zopiclone quickly, which is why it is usually prescribed for only 2 to 4 weeks.
The summary of product characteristics for zopiclone says treatment should stop immediately if a complex sleep behaviour such as sleepwalking occurs.
Zopiclone is a Class C drug in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations.
The NHS says zopiclone may not be suitable for people with sleep apnoea or other breathing problems, liver problems, muscle weakness, or a history of alcohol, drug or opioid addiction.
The NHS says dependence becomes more likely with longer use, and that a doctor or pharmacist can help someone come off zopiclone gradually, as sleep problems can temporarily return.
NICE notes that the risk of dependence and withdrawal should be considered when prescribing Z-drugs, and that rebound insomnia can occur on stopping.
In an emergency, such as a suspected overdose or severe withdrawal, call 999; NHS 111 or the GP can advise urgently; Samaritans on 116 123 is free at any time.

nitroimidazoles.summary: Antibiotic and antiparasitic medicines, including metronidazole and tinidazole, that act on bacteria and parasites. The NHS says metronidazole is an antibiotic used for bacterial infections, including skin infections, mouth infections, bacterial vaginosis and pelvic inflammatory disease, and is available only on prescription. MedlinePlus says tinidazole treats trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis, giardiasis and amoebiasis, and describes it as a nitroimidazole antimicrobial.
nitroimidazoles.mechanism: Microbial enzymes inside susceptible bacteria and parasites activate nitroimidazoles. The activated form then damages proteins and DNA. A study in Giardia found that metronidazole and tinidazole bind to the same subset of proteins. A therapeutic review says metronidazole has a limited spectrum that covers various protozoa and most anaerobic bacteria, and that it lacks efficacy against aerobic organisms. A review of tinidazole describes it as active in the laboratory against most clinically important anaerobic bacteria.
classEffects: LiverTox says tinidazole causes a low rate of raised liver enzymes during treatment, and rare cases of clinically apparent acute liver injury.
The NHS lists feeling or being sick, diarrhoea and a slight metallic taste in the mouth as common side effects of metronidazole.
MedlinePlus lists a sharp, unpleasant metallic taste among the side effects of tinidazole.
The NHS lists yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes among the rare but serious side effects of metronidazole.
cautions: For metronidazole, the NHS advises avoiding alcohol during treatment and for 2 days afterwards. Reactions listed include feeling or being sick, stomach pain, hot flushes, a pounding heartbeat and a headache.
NCBI LiverTox describes tinidazole as a nitroimidazole similar to metronidazole, with a likely similar range and frequency of side effects.
Tinidazole is broken down largely in the liver by an enzyme called CYP 3A4, which can lead to significant interactions with other medicines, according to LiverTox.

MedlinePlus advises avoiding alcohol and products containing alcohol during tinidazole treatment and for a period afterwards, as they may cause an upset stomach, vomiting, stomach cramps, headaches, sweating and flushing.
A review of alcohol and antibiotic interactions says the concern about alcohol with tinidazole rests on its chemical similarity to metronidazole, with no direct data identified.
MedlinePlus advises telling the doctor about kidney or liver disease before using metronidazole.

references.title: PubMed: Metronidazole. A therapeutic review and update
PubMed: Tinidazole in anaerobic infections: a review
PMC: Fact versus Fiction: a Review of the Evidence behind Alcohol and Antibiotic Interactions

alpha-blockers.summary: Alpha blockers, also called alpha-adrenoreceptor antagonists, are medicines that relax muscle; tamsulosin is used to relax the muscle around the bladder and prostate in an enlarged prostate. The NHS describes doxazosin as an alpha blocker used to lower high blood pressure, which can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke, and to treat symptoms of an enlarged prostate such as problems with peeing. A StatPearls review lists doxazosin, prazosin and terazosin as selective alpha-1 blockers used for high blood pressure, and describes them as second-line choices because of low blood pressure on standing.
alpha-blockers.mechanism: In an enlarged prostate, tamsulosin relaxes the muscle around the bladder and prostate gland, which makes it easier to pee. The NHS says doxazosin lowers blood pressure by widening the blood vessels. A StatPearls review explains that selective alpha-1 blockers widen blood vessels by stopping noradrenaline from activating alpha-1 receptors. A review says that non-selective alpha blockers also block presynaptic alpha-2 receptors, which normally reduce the release of noradrenaline.
classEffects: Dizziness or light-headedness, which a hospital leaflet notes may occur when first starting tamsulosin.
An allergic reaction to one alpha blocker, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin or terazosin, is a reason the NHS lists against tamsulosin.
For doxazosin the NHS lists headaches, swollen feet, ankles or fingers, needing to pee suddenly or more often, and lower stomach pain as the main side effects, which are usually mild and short-lived.
For tamsulosin the NHS lists dizziness and problems with ejaculation as the main side effects.
cautions: The NHS says other alpha blockers, such as doxazosin, alfuzosin, prazosin or terazosin, may lower blood pressure, and some blood pressure medicines may not mix well with tamsulosin.
Orthostatic hypotension, low blood pressure causing dizziness on standing, is listed by the NHS as a reason tamsulosin is not suitable.
The NHS also lists severe liver or kidney problems, planned cataract or glaucoma eye surgery and having fainted while urinating or just afterwards among the reasons tamsulosin may not be suitable.

For doxazosin, the NHS says dizziness is most likely when first starting or after a dose increase, and suggests avoiding alcohol at first; for tamsulosin it says alcohol can add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect and make dizziness worse. (cite also https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/tamsulosin/common-questions-about-tamsulosin/)
MedlinePlus says dizziness on standing up quickly is more common with doxazosin when treatment starts, when the dose is increased, or when treatment has been stopped for more than a few days.
The NHS says anyone due to have cataract or glaucoma surgery should tell the doctor in advance, because tamsulosin may cause complications during the operation.
The NHS says to tell a doctor or pharmacist about medicines for erectile dysfunction, such as sildenafil, tadalafil or vardenafil, when taking tamsulosin.

The NHS says to call NHS 111 after taking more than the prescribed amount of tamsulosin or doxazosin, because an extra dose can lower blood pressure and raise heart rate. (cite https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/tamsulosin/how-and-when-to-take-tamsulosin/ and https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/doxazosin/how-and-when-to-take-doxazosin/)

5-alpha-reductase-inhibitors.summary: A group of medicines that stop testosterone turning into the hormone DHT; finasteride, described by the NHS for an enlarged prostate and male pattern hair loss, is one of them. The MHRA has issued safety warnings about psychiatric side effects and sexual dysfunction for finasteride and dutasteride. MedlinePlus (a US source) says dutasteride is used to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia, an enlarged prostate gland, and belongs to the 5-alpha reductase inhibitors. The NHS says finasteride for hair loss is available only on a private prescription, not on the NHS.
5-alpha-reductase-inhibitors.mechanism: These medicines work by stopping testosterone, a sex hormone, turning into another hormone called dihydrotestosterone (DHT). Reviews describe dutasteride as blocking both type 1 and type 2 of the 5-alpha reductase enzyme, whereas finasteride mainly blocks type 2, and dutasteride lowers blood DHT further than finasteride does. A systematic review found insufficient evidence that either finasteride or dutasteride has an advantage over the other in efficacy or safety for clinically important outcomes.
classEffects: Sexual side effects such as losing interest in sex and difficulty getting an erection are the main side effects the NHS lists for finasteride, and some men report them continuing after stopping.
The MHRA says finasteride is associated with depression, suicidal thoughts and sexual dysfunction, and has added a precautionary warning for dutasteride.
StatPearls lists erection problems, reduced sex drive and difficulty ejaculating among the sexual side effects of dutasteride, and advises that breast enlargement or tenderness be reported.
StatPearls notes that sexual side effects may persist after dutasteride is stopped.
cautions: Finasteride can affect PSA blood test results, so the NHS advises telling the doctor about it if a PSA test is due.
For depression or suicidal thoughts, MHRA guidance for finasteride is to contact a healthcare professional urgently; if someone is in immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E.
The NHS says most men aged 18 or over can take finasteride, but it is generally not recommended for women or children.
The NHS lists depression or thoughts of self-harm, severe bladder problems and liver problems among the things to mention to the doctor before starting finasteride.
The NHS says it is very unlikely that a partner taking finasteride will harm a woman or her baby.
MedlinePlus (a US source) says dutasteride is for use only in men, and that women who are or may become pregnant should not handle dutasteride capsules.
The NHS says anyone with thoughts of harming themselves should call 999 or go to A&E; for low mood or distress, NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time, can help.
